name: Restricted Interests
summary: An intense, narrowly focused interest in a specific topic, object, or activity — extremely common in autistic people and often a genuine source of joy, comfort, and skill-building rather than something to be discouraged.
triggers: Not a 'trigger' in the problem sense — interests are typically self-chosen and intrinsically motivating
Stress or unfamiliar situations, where retreating to the interest offers comfort and predictability
Boredom or understimulation prompting a return to the familiar topic
Social or environmental cues that remind the person of the interest

remedies.text: Use the interest as a bridge to connection and learning — join in, ask questions, and use it to teach related skills rather than shutting it down
Set gentle, agreed-upon limits on timing (e.g. after homework, not during meals) rather than banning the interest outright
Help find peer groups or clubs centered on the same interest to build social connection around it
Social skills or flexibility coaching to help broaden conversation topics when needed for social situations, without requiring the interest itself to shrink

sources.label: Kennedy Krieger Institute (IAN) - Restricted Interests: Obsessions, 'Special Topics,' and Attention Deficits
PMC - Interests in high-functioning autism are more intense, interfering, and idiosyncratic, but not more circumscribed, than those in neurotypical development
